newsitem.title: FRANCE: France plans tax cuts to lift optimism.
newsitem.headline: France plans tax cuts to lift optimism.

text.p: France's conservative government, battling weak growth and high unemployment, was due on Thursday to announce deep income tax cuts to try to snap the country out of its gloomy mood.

Politicians who had discussed the tax plans with Prime Minister Alain Juppe said income tax revenue was likely to be reduced by 25 billion francs ($5 billion) next year while a total of 75 billion francs would be cut over the next five years.

While economists suggested some of that money would be recouped in higher taxes elsewhere, they said Juppe was clearly going to try to maximise the pyschological impact of cutting taxes to encourage consumer spending and boost growth.
"It may have a good effect on confidence. You end up with tax cuts which are not very big, but which are rather good news after a time of rising taxes," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.

France's economy, hit by an austerity drive in preparation for European monetary union, shrank in the second quarter after rising in the first quarter and looks to be on course for only modest growth over the whole of 1996.
The weakness in growth has created a vicious circle in which unemployment has hit spending, dampening growth further.
Officials said Juppe, whose government has raised both direct and indirect taxes since taking office, would present the tax cuts in a television broadcast at 8 pm (1800 GMT).

The size of the tax cuts expected next year will not be large -- they would roughly equal the money raised from a new flat 0.5 percent income tax, the RDS, imposed earlier this year to pay off accumulated welfare deficits.
And in purely economic terms they would far from offset some 60 billion francs in spending cuts expected to be made in a belt-tightening budget for 1997 to be announced on September 18.

"Tonight should be quite generous for the consumer but we will have to wait another two weeks to understand the full extent of the austerity," said Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais. "There will be a slight vacuum until then."

To maximise the impact, the government was therefore expected to focus on middle-income earners -- those most likely to spend their extra money -- rather than high-income earners who might just increase their savings.
At the same time the government must convince financial markets it has not slowed its drive to cut public spending ahead of the launch of a single European currency in 1999.
The government has pledged to reduce the total public deficit to four percent of gross domestic product product this year and three percent next year from five percent last year.
So far, economists are starting to believe if the government thinks it can cut taxes now, it is because they are confident of room to do so and still reach the three percent deficit target.
Government ministers have repeated in recent days that France will meet a Maastricht treaty requirement that deficits be reduced to three percent of GDP.
"The three percent definitely is convincing," Brossard said.
He noted that the government could be helped by a 37.5 billion franc payment from France Telecom to the state when it assumes its pension liabilities ahead of partial privatisation.
"This France Telecom money is going to be included as a surplus for the public sector, Therefore it gives some more room for manoeuvre than expected," Philippe Brossard.
The tax cuts are also likely to be offset by a rise in excise duties, particularly on alcohol and cigarettes, which economists said could raise between five and 10 billion francs.

The government is also expected to scrap a wide range of tax breaks over the next five years and reform savings taxes to shift what it calls "sleeping money" into productive investment in industry and the corporate sector.

For the government, the tax cuts could also boost its popularity and soothe a restive workforce, anxious about further public spending cuts, ahead of 1998 parliamentary elections. ($1=5.080 French Franc)
